item.title: Silent Evidence Loss Detector (SELD) spots hidden context deletions in LLMs
item.description:
Silent Evidence Loss Detector (SELD) spots hidden context deletions in LLMs

Context compression is now routine for language models with long inputs, but a compressed context is useful only if it keeps the evidence for the answer.

🔍 Overview

  • Existing checks compare the reader model’s answer or its most likely words, and thus miss a frequent failure, silent evidence loss.
  • Silent evidence loss occurs when key evidence is removed while the answer stays the same, leaving the answer unsupported and risky for other models that reuse the context.

🧩 How it works

  • SELD (Silent Evidence Loss Detector) needs no training and no labels.
  • Its principle is that when evidence is lost, a reader model’s preferences among the answers it leaves unsaid shift even if its answer does not.
  • By comparing these preferences before and after compression, SELD reveals losses that answer checks cannot see.

⚙️ Benchmark (SEL‑Pairs)

  • SEL‑Pairs is a benchmark of length‑matched evidence and control deletions from three question‑answering datasets.

🚀 Results

  • Quantitative and qualitative experiments with five reader models show that SELD consistently outperforms strong and recent baselines across compressors, compression rates and models.
  • SELD identifies the evidence‑removing edit in 83% of matched pairs with unchanged answers, against 70% for the strongest baseline.
  • These results show that evidence loss in compressed contexts can be detected even when the answer is unchanged.

💡 Why it matters

  • Detecting silent evidence loss prevents unsupported answers from being propagated to downstream models.
  • A training‑free detector can be applied to any compressor without additional data collection.

Submitted on 14 Oct 2026

#LLM #ContextCompression #Evaluation

item.title: FlexComp Introduces Any-Ratio Soft Context Compression for Large Language Models
item.description:
FlexComp Introduces Any-Ratio Soft Context Compression for Large Language Models

A new method-agnostic framework called FlexComp has been developed to decouple the compression ratio from the training and deployment of soft context compressors.

🔍 Overview

Soft context compression reduces a context into memory tokens for use by a frozen LLM. Previous compressors required separate models for each deployed ratio and applied a uniform ratio to all inputs regardless of their specific needs. FlexComp addresses these limitations by allowing a single model to function as an any-ratio compressor.

🧩 How it works

FlexComp utilizes Matryoshka-style training that samples the memory budget $K$ per instance. After training, the budget is selected per input using one of two methods:

Method Description
Confidence-based cascade routing Determines the budget based on confidence levels
Lightweight learned $K$ predictor Predicts the budget in a single compression-decoding pass

⚙️ Key details

Testing across SAC, 500xCompressor, and ICAE on MRQA showed that a single FlexComp model matches the performance of separately trained fixed-ratio specialists with minimal degradation. Performance metrics include:

  • Cascade routing: Maintains over 98% of the accuracy of the mildest ratio at an average compression of up to 266x.
  • $K$ predictor: Reaches 158-236x compression within 0.7 F1 of the mildest ratio.
  • Efficiency: At serving-scale batch sizes, the $K$ predictor improves decoding throughput by 47% and reduces the context KV cache by 50%.

#LLM #ContextCompression #FlexComp #MachineLearning

Source: FlexComp: One Model for Every Ratio in Context Compression
